meta.blurb: A courier feels faint on a hot July afternoon and asks the simplest question: what does water actually do? Follow Ben and his grandmother through one summer to learn how thirst works, how much to drink, and what is just a myth.
meta.bible: Ben: a bicycle courier of about twenty-nine, cheerful and always in a hurry, who delivers parcels across a hot city in July. Nell: Ben's grandmother, aged eighty-one, who lives alone, drinks little and is firmly independent. Zoe: Ben's colleague, a courier who is also studying sports science. Dr Mehta: Nell's family doctor, patient and practical. Maya: Ben's niece, aged seven. Lila: Ben's sister, who is expecting a baby. The story runs from July to October. Key terms: Water, Dehydration, Thirst, Hydration, Kidneys, Urine, Sweat, Sweating, Blood, Brain, Hormone, Sodium, Hyponatraemia, Electrolytes, Rehydration, Diuretic, Caffeine, Alcohol, Fluoride, Watermelon, Cucumber, Pregnancy, Dehydrated, Heatstroke. Facts used: an adult body is roughly half to six tenths water, babies more; water helps to control temperature, carry nutrients and waste, cushion joints and make saliva; we lose water in urine, sweat and breath, and gain it from drinks and from food, which supplies roughly a fifth; thirst starts when the brain senses the blood becoming more concentrated; the eight glasses a day rule has no strong scientific basis and needs vary with size, weather, activity and health; tea and coffee count towards fluid in normal amounts; alcohol makes the body lose more water; drinking far more than thirst asks for, especially during long endurance events, can dilute the blood's sodium, which is rare but serious; older adults feel thirst less strongly; during vomiting or diarrhoea the body loses water and salts and babies and older adults need advice early; people with some kidney, heart or liver conditions may be told to limit fluids by their doctor; the claim that water cures most illnesses is not supported by evidence. This book is general information and is not medical advice. Voice and tone: warm, clear, practical and gently funny; honest about what is uncertain; no invented numbers, studies or quotes; no diagnosis and no personal treatment advice.

B1B2: It is a very hot July afternoon, and Ben has been riding his courier bicycle since seven. Suddenly his head begins to ache, and the street seems to tilt a little.
Ben sits in the shade of a tree and realises that he has not had a single drink all day. He gulps down a bottle of water, and after ten minutes he feels much better.
That evening Ben tells his friend Zoe, who is a courier and also a sports science student. She smiles and says that she can explain a great deal about water and the body.
Zoe says that an adult body is roughly half to six tenths water. Babies have an even higher share, which is why they dry out so quickly when they are ill.
The water is not kept in just one big tank inside the body. It fills the tiny cells and the spaces around them, so almost every process in the body happens in water.
One job of water is to keep the body at the right temperature. When Ben is hot, his skin makes sweat, and as the sweat dries it carries heat away.
Blood is mostly water, and it carries food and oxygen to every part of the body. The kidneys then filter waste out of the blood and make it into urine.
Water is also part of the fluid that cushions the joints. It makes saliva for chewing and swallowing, and it helps food to move through the gut.
Zoe says that the body keeps a daily budget of water. Some comes in every day, some goes out, and the aim is to keep the two roughly equal.
Water leaves the body in urine and sweat, and also in every breath. Zoe breathes on a cold window and shows how the glass fogs up.
Water comes into the body from drinks, and also from food. Food gives roughly a fifth of the total, though that share varies from person to person.
Cucumber and watermelon are mostly water, with more than nine tenths of their weight coming from it. Soups, tomatoes, oranges and strawberries also add a useful amount.

Thirst starts in the brain, which keeps a careful watch on the blood. When the blood becomes a little more concentrated because there is less water in it, the brain notices and sends a signal to drink.
At the same time, the brain sends a hormone to the kidneys, telling them to save water. That is why the urine becomes darker when you have not had enough to drink.
For most healthy adults, thirst is a good guide. It starts early, when the body has lost only a small amount of water, long before anything dangerous happens.

Pale, straw-coloured urine usually suggests that you are well hydrated, and darker urine suggests that you need more fluid. Vitamins, some foods and some medicines can change the colour, so it is only a rough guide.
Mild dehydration can cause a dry mouth, tiredness, a headache and a feeling of dizziness. However, all of these signs have many other causes, so they prove nothing on their own.
Ben thinks about his dizzy afternoon, which probably had several causes. The heat, the hard riding and the lack of a drink were all likely to have played a part, although nobody can be sure.
Many people say that everybody must drink eight glasses of water a day. Zoe tells Ben that this rule has no strong scientific basis, and nobody is sure where it began.

In truth, the amount that people need changes with their size, the weather, their activity, their diet and their health. Official guides give different figures, so they are best treated as a rough guide.
Zoe says that tea and coffee count toward fluid too. The caffeine in them makes the body pass slightly more urine, but in normal amounts the effect is small.
Alcohol makes the body pass more urine, so it can leave you short of water. This is one reason why people often feel rough the morning after heavy drinking.
Plain water has no sugar and no calories, so it is kind to the teeth. In many places, tap water is cheap and safe, and some of it even contains fluoride to protect teeth.
When people work hard in the heat, they can sweat a litre or more in an hour, although this varies a lot. Ben decides to carry a bottle and to drink whenever he feels thirsty.
On very hot days, it helps to rest in the shade, wear light clothes and take regular breaks. Confusion, fainting or hot, dry skin can be signs of heatstroke, and they need urgent medical help.
During short or easy exercise, plain water is usually enough. In long events lasting several hours, drinks with salt and sugar can sometimes help, and athletes sometimes plan their drinking.
Drinking far more than you need can also be harmful, but this is rare. In very long events, too much plain water can dilute the sodium in the blood, a condition called hyponatraemia.
The kidneys can only clear so much water in an hour. So it is better to sip through the day than to force down litres in one go.
On Sundays Ben takes shopping to his grandmother, Nell, who is eighty-one and lives alone. Today she looks tired, and she admits that she drinks very little.
Zoe tells Ben that older adults often feel thirst less strongly than younger people. Their kidneys also save water less well, and some people drink less to avoid trips to the toilet.
Nell folds her arms and says that she has never been thirsty in her life. However, she agrees to talk to her doctor, Dr Mehta, if it will stop Ben from fussing.
Dr Mehta checks the list of medicines that Nell takes and listens to her story. In Nell's case, the doctor says, it is fine to drink regularly through the day.

Dr Mehta stresses that some people must limit their fluids, for example those with certain kidney, heart or liver conditions. For them, general advice does not apply, and they should follow their own doctor.
Ben puts a jug on Nell's table and fills it every morning. Tea counts too, so she sets out a few small cups and drinks a little at a time.
When a person has vomiting or diarrhoea, the body loses water and salts quickly. Special rehydration drinks can help, and babies and older adults should get medical advice early.
Ben's niece Maya, who is seven, has a bright new water bottle for school. Children lose water quickly in play, and they often forget to drink unless somebody reminds them.

Ben's sister Lila is expecting her second baby in December, and she is delighted. During pregnancy, and while breastfeeding, the body needs a little more fluid than usual, so Lila keeps a glass beside her.
Some people claim that almost every ache and illness is caused by thirst and cured by water. Scientists have not found good evidence for that, and it can be dangerous to ignore real symptoms.

In some people, not drinking enough seems to trigger headaches, although the evidence is mixed. Anyone who has frequent or severe headaches should see a doctor, and a glass of water is not a good test.
Some small studies suggest that mild dehydration can slightly lower concentration and mood. The effects seem small, and most people who drink when thirsty will not notice them.
Many people say that extra water gives them better skin. In people who are already well hydrated, the evidence for this is weak, although severe dehydration can leave skin looking dry.
Doctors often advise people who get kidney stones to drink plenty of fluid. Drinking more makes the urine more dilute, which makes it less likely that stones will form.
Fluid and fibre work together to keep the gut moving. If mild dehydration is part of a person's constipation, drinking enough may help, but fibre is usually just as important.
Easy habits work best, so Zoe keeps the plan simple and kind. Carry a bottle, drink a glass with each meal, and add a slice of lemon or cucumber if plain water seems dull.
In many places, tap water is safe, cheap and easy to refill. Where it is not safe, people should use boiled or treated water, and look for local advice.
Two weeks later, Nell seems brighter, and she tells Ben that she feels less tired. Dr Mehta says that several things may explain it, and drinking more is only one of them.
Ben now takes a sip from his bottle at every delivery. He has not felt dizzy again, and his headaches are gone, although he knows that this is only his own experience.
In October the weather turns cool, and Ben sweats much less on his rounds. He still drinks when he is thirsty, and he keeps his bottle, because heated rooms can dry the body too.
Ben writes a short list of what he has learned. Drink when you are thirsty, check the colour of your urine, take more in heat and illness, and never force down litres.
This book gives general information about water, and it is not medical advice. Anyone with a health condition, or a worry about their drinking, should speak to a doctor.
C1C2: It was a blazing July afternoon, and Ben, who had been delivering parcels by bicycle since seven in the morning, suddenly felt the street lurch beneath him. A dull ache gathered behind his eyes, his mouth tasted like paper, and the cheerful rhythm of his legs deserted him. He steered to the kerb and put one foot down, wondering what on earth had happened.

In the shade of a plane tree, Ben worked out that he had not had a single drink since a cup of coffee at breakfast. He emptied a bottle in a few long swallows, sat quietly while his pulse settled, and noticed that the world slowly grew steadier and sharper. It was a modest sort of miracle, he thought, but it made him curious about what exactly the water had been doing inside him.

That evening, over tea at the depot, Ben described the whole episode to Zoe, a fellow courier who spent her spare hours studying sports science. She listened with the satisfied air of someone who had been waiting for precisely this question, and she promised to explain everything the body does with water, from the first sip to the last drop. Ben, still slightly sheepish about the whole affair, said that he was ready to learn, and that he had a notebook somewhere in his bag.

Zoe began with a striking fact, which was that an adult body is made up of roughly half to six tenths water, with the exact share depending on age, build and sex. Babies contain an even higher proportion, she added, and the proportion slowly falls as we grow older and our muscle gives way to fat. Ben looked down at his arms as though seeing them for the first time.

The body does not keep its water in a single tank, Zoe explained, but spreads it through the cells and the spaces between them, in the blood and in the fluid around every organ. Almost every chemical process in the body takes place in water, so it is less like a drink that we pour into a container and more like the medium in which we live. Ben thought that this was a remarkable idea for a Tuesday evening, and he found himself looking at his own hands with new respect.

One of the most important jobs of water, Zoe said, is to keep the body at a steady temperature, and sweat is the cooling system that does it. As the moisture evaporates from the skin it carries heat away, rather as a wet cloth cools a bottle, and a person working hard in the heat may need to replace a good deal of it. Ben, who had been sweating since seven, felt a new respect for his own skin.

Blood is mostly water, Zoe explained, and it carries nutrients and oxygen to every corner of the body while collecting the waste that cells produce. The kidneys filter this waste from the blood and dissolve it in a little water to make urine, and they adjust how much water is used for the job according to the body's needs. They are, she said, quietly one of the cleverest organs that we own, and almost nobody ever stops to thank them.

Water has a number of quieter duties, Zoe continued, such as forming part of the lubricating fluid that cushions the joints and making the saliva that helps us chew and swallow. It also helps to move food along the digestive system, and it carries dissolved salts that nerves and muscles need in order to work. Ben realised that his body had been performing all of this without once asking for credit.

The simplest way to understand hydration, Zoe said, is as a daily budget in which water comes in and water goes out, and the body's aim is to keep the two roughly equal. Most days the books balance quite well without any conscious effort, and the trouble begins only when the outgoings suddenly rise, as they do in hot weather, in illness or during hard exercise. Ben, who had never kept a budget of any kind, found this oddly appealing.

Water leaves the body in several ways, Zoe said, mostly in urine, but also in sweat, in a small amount of solid waste and even in the breath. To prove the last point she breathed on the cold window of the depot, and a small cloud of mist spread across the glass and slowly faded. Ben admitted that he had never thought of breathing as a way of losing water.

Water enters the body not only through drinks, Zoe pointed out, but through food, which supplies roughly a fifth of the total for many people. The exact share depends on the diet, and someone who eats a great many fruits, vegetables and soups takes in a good deal more than someone who lives on dry biscuits. Ben, who lived mainly on sandwiches and the occasional banana, resolved on the spot to eat a few more vegetables.

Some foods are astonishingly watery, and cucumber and watermelon are both made up of more than nine tenths water by weight. Soups, tomatoes, oranges and strawberries have a high share as well, so a summer lunch of salad and fruit contributes a noticeable amount to the daily budget. Ben, who had always thought of watermelon as dessert, now saw it as a drink with a rind.

Thirst, Zoe told him, is not a simple dryness of the mouth, but a message sent from the brain, which keeps a careful watch on the blood. When the blood becomes slightly more concentrated because the body has less water in it, special sensors notice the change and the brain produces the unmistakable urge to drink. It is one of the most reliable alarm systems that we possess, and it has been working since the day we were born.

At the same moment, the brain releases a hormone that travels in the blood to the kidneys with an instruction to hold on to water. The kidneys obey by producing less urine, and because the same amount of waste is dissolved in less water, the urine becomes darker, which makes it a useful signal. Ben, who had never studied his own plumbing before, took out his notebook and began to write down the words that he did not know.

For most healthy adults, Zoe said, thirst is a dependable guide, since it arrives early, when the body has lost only a small fraction of its water. It is not a sign that something has already gone seriously wrong, and in everyday life a person who drinks when thirsty will usually be well hydrated. The sensible response to the alarm, she said, is simply to answer it, with a drink of water and no great drama.

A quick check that anyone can make, Zoe suggested, is to glance at the colour of the urine, since a pale straw shade usually points to good hydration and a deeper amber suggests the need for more water. It is only a rough guide, however, because vitamin pills, beetroot and certain medicines can alter the colour without any connection to hydration. She advised him to treat it as a clue and never as a verdict.

Mild dehydration can bring a dry mouth, tiredness, a headache and a feeling of light-headedness, Zoe said, and these were exactly the symptoms that had troubled Ben on the road. Every one of them, however, has many other possible causes, from lack of sleep to illness, so none of them can prove that someone is short of water. She was careful, she said, never to jump to conclusions about a stranger's body.

Thinking back to his dizzy afternoon, Ben concluded that it had probably been the result of several causes working together, among them the heat, hard exercise, a skipped lunch and an empty bottle. Zoe agreed that dehydration was a likely contributor, but she added that nobody can be certain from a distance, and that a person who feels seriously unwell should see a doctor and not guess. It seemed to Ben a very fair answer, and a good deal more honest than the confident certainty of most websites.

Everyone has heard the rule that we must drink eight glasses of water a day, Zoe said, but there is no strong scientific evidence behind it. Nobody is quite certain where the idea began, and it seems to have spread as a handy slogan long before anyone tested it, though its heart was not unreasonable. Ben, who had been feeling guilty for years about glass number five, felt his shoulders relax.

How much a person needs depends on body size, climate, activity, diet and health, Zoe explained, and no single number can fit a retired librarian and a courier in July. Official guides suggest different totals, some of which count only drinks and others of which include the water in food, so any figure is really only a starting point. Pay attention to thirst and to the colour of the urine, she said, and adjust.

A pleasant surprise, Zoe told him, was that tea and coffee count toward the daily fluid total, since they are mostly water. Caffeine has a mild diuretic effect, meaning that it makes the kidneys produce slightly more urine, but in the amounts that most people drink the effect is small and does not cancel the benefit of the fluid. Ben, who drank at least three cups of tea or coffee every day without fail, was visibly and enormously relieved.

Alcohol behaves differently from tea and coffee, Zoe warned, because it suppresses the brain's signal that tells the kidneys to save water, and the drinker therefore passes a great deal of urine. This loss is one of several reasons why a person feels so wretched the morning after heavy drinking, though it is not the only cause of a hangover. A glass of water between alcoholic drinks, she said, is a cheap and sensible precaution that costs nothing and saves a great deal of misery.

Plain water has the advantage that it contains no sugar and no calories, which makes it kinder to the teeth than fizzy drinks and sweetened juices. In many countries tap water is safe, cheap and sometimes treated with fluoride, a mineral that helps to protect tooth enamel, and it costs a tiny fraction of what the bottled kind does. Ben, who spent a small fortune each month on cold drinks, did some quiet arithmetic.

In hot weather and hard physical work, Zoe said, some people can sweat a litre or more in a single hour, though the amount varies enormously from person to person. This was enough to persuade Ben to fasten a large bottle to his bicycle frame and to sip from it whenever his thirst spoke up. It was, he decided, the least that a man in his line of work could do.

On the hottest days, Zoe advised, sensible workers rest in the shade, wear light clothing, take regular breaks and drink to thirst. Heatstroke is far more serious than simple thirst, and signs such as confusion, fainting, a very high temperature or hot, dry skin need urgent medical help and not just a glass of water. Ben copied that sentence into his notebook and underlined it, because it was the one that mattered most.

For ordinary exercise lasting an hour or less, Zoe said, plain water is generally all that the body needs, along with a normal meal later. During long events that last several hours, drinks which contain salts and a little sugar can be useful, and some athletes plan their drinking carefully in advance. Most of us, she said with a smile, never come anywhere near that situation, and we can safely leave the marathon runners to their sums.

Too much water can also cause harm, Zoe warned, although the problem is rare and occurs mostly in very long endurance events. If someone drinks far more than thirst demands, the sodium in the blood becomes diluted, a condition called hyponatraemia, which can cause headache, confusion and in extreme cases serious illness. Drinking to thirst, she said, is the best protection against it, and it is a rule that even a very tired courier can remember.

The kidneys, however efficient, can remove only a limited amount of water in an hour, which is why there are limits to how much anyone can safely drink at once. A steady habit of sipping through the day is far better than forcing down several litres in an afternoon, and drinking beyond thirst seldom brings any benefit to a healthy adult. Ben, who had once drunk two litres in ten minutes for a bet, felt a flash of retrospective alarm.

On Sundays, Ben carried a bag of shopping up three flights of stairs to the flat of his grandmother Nell, who was eighty-one and fiercely independent. That week she seemed tired and a little vague, and when he asked what she had been drinking she waved a hand and said that she hardly bothered, because it only meant more trips along the corridor. Ben, who had been studying hydration all month, felt something tighten in his chest.

When Ben described his grandmother's habits, Zoe explained that older adults frequently feel thirst less strongly than the young, and that their kidneys also become less able to conserve water. Some drink too little on purpose to avoid trips to the bathroom, and some take medicines that increase the need for fluid, so the risk of dehydration is higher than people suppose. None of this, she said gently, is anyone's fault, and it is simply what happens to thirst and kidneys as the years go by.

Nell, who had survived eighty-one years without anyone's advice, folded her arms and declared that she had never been thirsty in her life and did not intend to begin now. After a good deal of negotiation, and the promise of a Sunday cake, she agreed to mention the matter to her doctor, which at least left the decision in the hands of someone who knew her medical history. Ben accepted this small victory with a perfectly straight face, which was harder than it sounds in front of a grandmother of her experience.

Dr Mehta, a patient woman with a large collection of pens, went carefully through Nell's list of medicines and asked about her appetite, her sleep and her habits. Nell's own circumstances were taken into account before any advice was given, and the doctor concluded that regular drinks spread across the day would suit her well. Ben, waiting in the corridor, was relieved to learn that the visit had been so uneventful.

Before Nell left, Dr Mehta emphasised a point that she made to everybody, which was that general advice about drinking cannot fit every body. People with certain kidney, heart or liver conditions are sometimes told to limit their fluids, she said, and anyone in that position must follow the advice of their own doctor instead of anything that they read. Ben wrote this down too, in capital letters, because it seemed to him the most important sentence in the entire conversation.

Ben's solution for Nell was gloriously simple, namely a jug on the table beside her chair, filled each morning, with a few small cups next to it. Tea and milky coffee counted as well, he assured her, and small, regular drinks suited her better than a heroic gulp, since they did not require a rush to the bathroom. Nell, who disliked being managed and said so often, was grudgingly impressed by the engineering, and she poured her first cup before he had left.

During a stomach illness with vomiting or diarrhoea, the body can lose water and salts at a startling rate, and the loss matters most in babies, young children and older adults. Oral rehydration drinks, which are made from a careful balance of salts and sugar, can help in mild cases, but anyone who cannot keep fluids down, or who seems drowsy or confused, needs medical advice early. Zoe said that speed is far more important than pride in such cases, and that nobody should feel foolish for asking for help early.

Ben's niece Maya, who was seven, proudly displayed the bright bottle that she now carried to school each morning. Small bodies lose water quickly in hot weather and busy play, and children are notorious for forgetting to drink while they are enjoying themselves, so a bottle and a gentle reminder from a teacher can make a real difference. Maya treated the bottle as a trophy, and Ben thought that this was exactly the right attitude.

Ben's sister Lila was expecting her second baby, and she told him, with the weary air of an expert, that she had been advised to keep a glass of water close at hand. A pregnant woman needs a little more fluid than usual to support the baby and the extra blood that she carries, and a breastfeeding mother needs a little more again. Her own doctor or midwife, Lila added, would know what was right for her.

Zoe warned Ben about a claim that he would certainly meet online, namely that almost every ache, pain and serious illness is a cry for water and can be cured by drinking more. Scientists have found no good evidence for this, and it can be dangerous, because someone who treats a real symptom with a glass of water may delay seeing a doctor. Water is essential for life, she said, but it is not a cure for everything.

In some people, being short of fluid does seem to bring on headaches, Zoe said, although the research is mixed and it is not clear how large the effect is. Headaches are extremely common and have many causes, and anyone with frequent, severe or unusual headaches should see a doctor and not simply drink more water. Ben, who had expected a clean and simple answer, found himself respecting the complexity.

Some small studies have suggested that mild dehydration may slightly reduce concentration, alertness and mood, particularly in hot conditions or during exercise. The effects appear to be small, however, and a person who drinks whenever thirst appears is unlikely to notice them, so there is no need to treat a glass of water as a performance drug. Zoe held up a hand and warned that these were early findings and not yet final.

Another popular belief, Zoe said, is that drinking extra water gives the skin a youthful glow, but the evidence for this is weak in people who are already well hydrated. Severe dehydration can certainly leave the skin looking dry and slack, yet once the body has enough fluid, a further glass does not seem to add anything, and a good moisturiser may do rather more. Ben thought that this was refreshingly honest, and rather better than the glowing promises that he had seen on the labels of expensive bottles.

One area in which the advice to drink more is well supported, Zoe said, concerns kidney stones, which can form when minerals in the urine become too concentrated. Doctors therefore often advise people who have had stones to drink plenty of fluid, so that the urine stays dilute and stones become less likely to form. Ben wondered how many people had learned this particular lesson in rather painful circumstances, and he made a mental note to tell his uncle.

The gut, Zoe explained, relies on both fluid and fibre to keep things moving, and a person who is mildly dehydrated may find that constipation is worse than it need be. Drinking enough can help, but fibre from fruit, vegetables, beans and wholegrain foods is usually just as important, and persistent bowel problems deserve a visit to the doctor. Ben, blushing slightly at the subject, decided that on his way home he would buy some oats, a few apples and a bag of lentils.

Zoe's advice on habit was gloriously practical: carry a bottle where you can see it, drink a glass with each meal, and sip whenever you pass a tap or a fountain. If plain water seems dull, she said, a slice of lemon, a few mint leaves or a piece of cucumber makes it more inviting, and the aim is steady sipping and not heroic effort. Ben fastened his new bottle to the bicycle frame with a cheerful snap, and felt like a man who had at last been properly equipped.

In many countries tap water is carefully tested, safe to drink and far cheaper than bottled water, and refilling a bottle from the tap also reduces the amount of plastic that is thrown away. In places where the water supply is not safe, however, people should drink water that has been boiled or properly treated, and they should follow local advice. Zoe said that safety comes first and economy comes second, and she added that nobody ever regretted boiling a kettle.

Two weeks later, Nell opened the door to Ben with a lively expression, announced that she felt less tired, and invited him in as if he were a visiting dignitary. Dr Mehta, when asked, said that several things might explain the improvement, including more regular drinking, better sleep and the pleasure of a daily routine, and that nobody could say which mattered most. Ben decided that he did not much care which it was, since all of the explanations pointed toward a happier grandmother.

Ben made a habit of taking a sip at every delivery, which cost him almost no time and became as automatic as locking his bicycle. Over the remaining weeks of the summer he did not once feel dizzy or headachy on the road, though he was careful to add that this was his own experience and proved nothing. It was, he thought, an uncomplicated change with a pleasant result, and he felt a little like a scientist who had run an experiment on himself.

By October the weather had cooled, the leaves were falling in the wet streets, and Ben was sweating far less on his rounds, so he naturally drank rather less. The habit did not disappear, however, because indoor heating can dry the air and the body, and thirst remained as faithful a guide in October as it had been in July. He no longer needed a rule, he realised, because he had learned to listen.

Ben wrote down everything that he had learned in a short list for Zoe, and it began with the simplest rule of all: drink when you are thirsty. Check the colour of the urine, he went on, take a little more in heat, illness and hard exercise, ask a doctor if you have a condition that affects fluids, and never force down far more than you need. Zoe read it through, nodded and handed back the notebook without a single correction.

On a quiet Sunday in October, Ben and Nell sat together over tea, with the jug of water between them and the autumn light on the table. This book gives general information only and is not medical advice, so anyone who has a health condition, who takes regular medicines or who has any worry about how much they drink should speak to a doctor. For everyone else, the next step is to pour a glass and enjoy it.
